course.learn: Injection occurs when untrusted input is interpreted as code, commands, or query syntax by another system. The underlying problem is mixing data with executable instructions.
course.why: Injection can let an attacker make the application perform operations the developer never intended.
course.example: A web form passes raw user input directly into a SQL statement, allowing the user to append database commands.
course.exam: SQL, command, and LDAP injection all share the same idea: unsafe input changes the structure of an interpreter/query.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: SQL injection changes a database query by inserting malicious SQL through application input. Prepared/parameterized queries keep user data separate from SQL syntax.
course.why: Database compromise can expose or modify large amounts of sensitive information.
course.example: The input `' OR 1=1 --` changes an unsafe login query so its condition always evaluates true.
course.exam: Best mitigation: parameterized/prepared queries. WAF can help, but secure coding fixes the root cause.

defs: Cross-Site Scripting: malicious client-side script executes in another user’s browser.

course.learn: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) lets attacker-controlled script execute in another user's browser in the context of a trusted site.
course.why: The browser may give that script access to session data or the ability to perform actions as the victim.
course.example: A comment field stores unsanitized JavaScript, and every user who views the page runs the attacker's script.
course.exam: XSS targets the browser/client. Output encoding and safe templating are core mitigations.

course.learn: Command injection occurs when untrusted input is passed to an operating-system shell or command interpreter and becomes part of an executable command.
course.why: Successful command injection can give attackers direct system-level capabilities.
course.example: A diagnostic web page runs `ping ` plus user input; the attacker appends shell syntax to run another command.
course.exam: Shell/OS commands = command injection. Use safe APIs, input validation, and avoid invoking a shell with raw user data.

course.learn: LDAP injection alters an LDAP directory query by supplying input that changes the intended filter or command structure.
course.why: It can bypass authentication or expose directory information when applications build LDAP queries unsafely.
course.example: A login form concatenates untrusted input into an LDAP filter, allowing a crafted value to match unintended accounts.
course.exam: Same root problem as SQL injection, but the target interpreter/query language is LDAP.

defs: A memory-safety flaw where more data is written into a buffer than it was designed to hold.

course.learn: A buffer overflow happens when software writes more data into a memory region than it was designed to hold, potentially corrupting adjacent memory and control data.
course.why: Memory corruption can crash programs or allow arbitrary code execution and privilege escalation.
course.example: An application copies an oversized network field into a fixed-length stack buffer without bounds checking.
course.exam: Memory-safety flaw + oversized input = buffer overflow. Modern mitigations include safe languages/APIs, bounds checks, ASLR, DEP/NX, and stack protections.

course.learn: Replay attacks capture valid data or authentication material and transmit it again later so the receiver accepts an old action as new.
course.why: If a protocol does not prove freshness, an attacker may not need to know the underlying secret.
course.example: A captured authentication request is resent later and accepted because the protocol uses no nonce or timestamp.
course.exam: Freshness controls such as nonces, timestamps, sequence numbers, and short-lived tokens help stop replay.

course.learn: Privilege escalation occurs when an attacker moves from lower privileges to higher privileges, such as from a normal user to administrator/root.
course.why: Higher privilege increases the attacker's ability to disable defenses, access sensitive data, and persist.
course.example: A local vulnerability lets a standard user execute code as SYSTEM.
course.exam: The key clue is gaining more permission than originally authorized.

defs: Ensuring data stays accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized modification.

course.learn: Forgery creates or alters data, documents, messages, tokens, or transactions so they appear legitimate when they are not.
course.why: Successful forgery undermines integrity and trust in the system's evidence.
course.example: An attacker modifies a payment instruction and creates a fake approval token that appears to come from an authorized user.
course.exam: Digital signatures, integrity checks, authenticated protocols, and protected audit trails help detect or prevent forgery.

course.learn: Directory traversal manipulates file paths so an application accesses files outside the intended directory, often using sequences such as `../`.
course.why: If path validation is weak, an attacker may read configuration files, credentials, or other sensitive content.
course.example: A download parameter meant for report.pdf is changed to ../../etc/passwd.
course.exam: File path escapes intended folder = directory traversal/path traversal.
